name: Take LTL pickup requests
function: LTL terminal operations and customer service
summary: Shippers ask the carrier to collect freight by phoning or emailing the local terminal, calling central customer service, entering a request on the web portal or by EDI, or through a standing daily pickup. A terminal service clerk or customer service representative finds the account, records the ready and closing times, pieces, weight and special needs such as a liftgate, and the TMS checks credit holds, the destination and the same-day cutoff before posting the pickup on the terminal's board for the city dispatcher. Most requests take a few minutes of hands-on work; delays come from late-afternoon calls past the cutoff, portal requests sent overnight, and missing details such as dock hours or a liftgate, which surface later as failed pickups.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian LTL and truckload carrier of about 3,000 employees with 38 terminals, a central customer service team and a TMS with a customer portal.
baseline.notes: About 100,000 pickup requests a month across 38 terminals, roughly 120 per terminal per business day, with large differences between hub cities and small terminals.

trigger: A shipper phones, emails, enters a portal or EDI request, or a standing daily pickup order comes due.
end_state: The pickup has a confirmation number and sits on the terminal pickup board for its pickup date, or it was declined for credit or cancelled by the shipper.

volume.seasonality: Autumn peak from September to mid-December; lower in late December, early January and the summer holiday weeks. Mondays and the day before a long weekend run heaviest, and within the day requests peak late morning and early afternoon before the cutoff.

evidence.note: Taken from the organisation file's process map entry (derived from 150,000 shipments a month at about 1.5 shipments per pickup stop).

surge.cause: Autumn shipping peak (September to mid-December retail and industrial restocking)

evidence.note: LTL volumes in Canada rise from September to early December; author's estimate of size.
About 45 terminal service clerks in the organisation file; taking pickups is their largest task, alongside traces, paperwork and driver check-in. Share is the author's estimate.
About 60 customer service representatives; pickup calls and credit-hold and cash-account cases are a minority of their work next to tracing and billing questions. Author's estimate.
Dispatchers decide late pickups only; most of their time is in route planning and dispatch. Author's estimate.

systems.name: Transportation management system (LTL and truckload operations, billing, rating)
Customer web portal (pickup requests, tracing, documents)
EDI gateway (204 tenders, 211 bills of lading, 214 status, 210 invoices)
Email, phone system and contact centre software
City route planning and dispatch board

steps.name: Sort incoming request by channel
steps.description: The request reaches the carrier by one of four routes: a phone call or email to the local terminal, a call to the central customer service line, a web portal or EDI request, or a standing daily pickup that the shipper set up once. The phone system and the TMS route each one to the right queue without a person touching it.
inputs: shipper call, email, portal entry, EDI message or standing order

next.condition: phone call or email to the terminal

evidence.note: Channel shares are the author's estimate for a Canadian LTL carrier in 2019-2022: most small shippers still phoned or emailed the terminal, larger shippers used the portal or EDI, and regular shippers had standing daily pickups. FedEx Freight Canada and CSA Transportation offer web, phone and terminal channels (src-fedex-pickup, src-csa-ltl were read for the channel list, not the shares).

steps.name: Answer shipper call or email at the terminal
steps.description: The terminal service clerk picks up the call on the terminal line or opens the email in the shared pickup inbox. They note the caller's company, pickup address and contact, and ask whether this is a new pickup, a change or a trace question.

evidence.note: Author's estimate: calls cluster in late morning and after lunch, so callers wait on hold or emails sit up to 45 minutes in the inbox.

steps.name: Find the shipper account in the TMS
steps.description: The clerk searches the TMS by account number, company name or phone number and checks that the pickup address on file matches. Shippers without an account, such as a one-off or residential shipper, are passed to central customer service to set one up.

error.defect_description: Wrong account or wrong pickup address selected.

next.condition: no account: new or one-time shipper

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Key the pickup details
steps.description: The clerk types the ready and close times, number of pallets or pieces, weight, dimensions of long or oversized pieces, destination postal code, dangerous goods flag and special services such as liftgate, inside pickup or residential access. These details decide which truck and how much time the dispatcher allows.

error.defect_description: Dock hours, liftgate need or piece count missing or wrong, which leads to a failed or slow pickup.

evidence.note: The fields are those carriers ask for (ready and close times, weight, handling units, liftgate). Touch time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Take the call at central customer service
steps.description: A customer service representative answers an overflow or toll-free call in the contact centre, identifies the caller and confirms the pickup city and terminal that will serve it.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Find the account from the contact centre
steps.description: The representative looks up the account in the TMS and checks the pickup address. Without local knowledge of the shipper's dock they rely on the notes in the account record.

error.defect_description: Wrong account or pickup address selected.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Key the pickup details from the contact centre
steps.description: The representative enters the same pickup fields as a terminal clerk: ready and close times, pieces, weight, destination, dangerous goods and special services, then saves the request to the serving terminal's queue.

error.defect_description: Special needs such as liftgate or dock closing time missed because the representative does not know the site.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Load the portal or EDI request into the terminal queue
steps.description: The customer portal or the EDI gateway writes the shipper's request into the TMS and places it in the serving terminal's queue for review. Requests sent in the evening or on weekends wait there until the terminal office opens.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Review the portal or EDI request
steps.description: The clerk opens each queued request and checks that the ready time, closing time, weight and piece count make sense together, that a liftgate is requested where the address has no dock, and that dangerous goods are flagged. Complete requests are released; incomplete ones need a call.

error.defect_description: Implausible weight or missing liftgate not noticed.

evidence.note: The checks follow the fields carriers require online. Wait: requests entered after the office closes wait overnight for the extended-hours clerks (author's estimate).

steps.name: Call the shipper for missing details
steps.description: The clerk phones or emails the shipping contact to get the missing dock hours, liftgate need, piece count or dangerous goods information and updates the request. When nobody answers, the clerk books the pickup with what it has and adds a note for the driver.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Generate the standing daily pickup
steps.description: Before the office opens, the TMS creates today's pickup for every shipper with a standing daily or weekly pickup order, using the details stored when the order was set up.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Set up a cash account and key the pickup
steps.description: Central customer service creates a prepaid or collect cash account for a shipper without credit, explains that the freight must be prepaid or billed to a consignee with an account, and keys the pickup.

error.defect_description: Bill-to party or payment terms recorded wrongly.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Check the account for a credit hold
steps.description: The TMS compares the account with the collections team's credit hold list and blocks the pickup if the account is over its limit or past due.

control.basis: Company credit policy: no service to accounts on credit hold without collections release

evidence.note: Author's estimate: about 1 to 2% of requests hit a credit hold.

steps.name: Resolve the credit hold with the shipper
steps.description: A customer service representative tells the shipper the pickup is on hold and passes the case to collections. The pickup goes ahead once payment or a release is confirmed; otherwise it is cancelled.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Validate the destination against the service area
steps.description: The TMS checks the destination postal code against the carrier's service-point table and marks shipments that go beyond the network to an interline partner or cartage agent, or to ferry and remote points.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Flag the beyond-point shipment
steps.description: The clerk adds a note to the pickup that the freight moves to an interline partner or cartage agent and tells the shipper about the longer transit time and extra charge.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Check the same-day cutoff
steps.description: The TMS compares the request time and ready time with the terminal's same-day cutoff, usually 2 or 3 p.m. local time, and with the zone's remaining pickup capacity that the dispatcher has set.

evidence.note: Cutoffs of 3 p.m. (FedEx Freight Canada) and 2 p.m. (CSA Transportation) for same-day pickup; the 14% share of late requests is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Decide whether a late pickup can run today
steps.description: The city dispatcher looks at the route board for a driver near the address with time left before the shipper closes and before the driver's on-duty limit, and accepts or refuses the late pickup.

evidence.note: Same-day service after the cutoff is checked by phone with the local terminal; the acceptance share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Move the pickup to the next business day
steps.description: The clerk calls or emails the shipper to say the pickup will run the next business day, changes the pickup date in the TMS and notes any delivery promise that now slips.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Assign pickup number and post to the pickup board
steps.description: The TMS gives the request a pickup confirmation number and places it on the terminal's pickup board under the city zone for the pickup date, where the dispatcher sees it.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Confirm the pickup number to the shipper
steps.description: For phone and email requests the clerk reads or emails the confirmation number to the shipper; portal and EDI shippers get an automatic confirmation. Some shippers call back before the driver arrives to change the ready time or cancel.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Change or cancel the pickup
steps.description: The clerk opens the pickup, changes the ready time, pieces or special services, or cancels it, and tells the dispatcher if a driver has already been given the stop.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

exceptions.name: Missing details on a portal or EDI request
exceptions.description: The request lacks dock hours, liftgate or pieces and the clerk has to call the shipper before releasing it.

exceptions.name: Late request after the same-day cutoff
exceptions.description: The request comes in after 2 or 3 p.m. or the zone is full; the dispatcher accepts about half and the rest move to the next business day.

exceptions.name: Account on credit hold
exceptions.description: Collections has stopped service; the pickup waits for payment or is cancelled.

exceptions.name: New shipper without an account
exceptions.description: Customer service sets up a cash account before the pickup is booked.

exceptions.name: Shipper changes or cancels
exceptions.description: The shipper calls back to change the ready time or cancel; cancellations after the driver has the stop waste route capacity.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from request received to pickup posted on the board
benchmarks.population: Canadian LTL pickup requests, all channels, 2019-2022

evidence.note: Author's estimate: phone requests are posted within minutes; portal and EDI requests sent after hours wait overnight for the terminal office, which drives the 90th percentile.

benchmarks.population: Canadian LTL carriers' published same-day pickup cutoffs

evidence.note: FedEx Freight Canada 3 p.m.; CSA Transportation 2 p.m. (current pages, practice assumed unchanged since 2019).

benchmarks.unit: minutes between ready time and close time
benchmarks.population: FedEx Freight Canada online pickup requests

evidence.note: Stated on the FedEx Freight Canada pickup page.

pain_points.description: Requests arrive after the cutoff or with closing times too early for the route, so dispatch rolls them or squeezes them into afternoon routes.

evidence.note: Cutoffs are published; the pressure on afternoon routes is the author's observation of common practice.

pain_points.description: Dock hours, liftgate needs and piece counts are often missing or wrong, which shows up only when the driver arrives and causes attempted pickups and rework.

evidence.note: Carriers charge for attempted pickups and liftgate service, showing these are recurring problems; frequency is the author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Phone and email requests are re-keyed by hand into the TMS, and the same shipper may call the terminal and customer service for the same pickup, creating duplicates.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

sources.title: Schedule a FedEx Freight pickup
sources.supports: General cutoff of 3 p.m. for automated pickup requests; online ready time no later than 3 p.m. local; same-day requests after 3 p.m. by phone to customer support or the local service centre; pickups booked same day or up to 10 business days ahead; request needs ready and close times at least 90 minutes apart, weight, number of handling units, package type and special services such as liftgate (no dock means a liftgate is needed); requests by web tool, phone or local service centre.

sources.title: LTL freight shipping
sources.supports: Canadian LTL carrier offering same-day pickup for orders placed before 2 PM local time; pickups requested by online form or by converting quotes to pickup requests in the client portal; freight is picked up, consolidated at the nearest terminal with other shipments for the same region, moved on scheduled lanes and delivered.

sources.title: Terms and Conditions - Tariff 101 (16th revision, effective April 14, 2025)
sources.supports: Canadian domestic LTL rules under provincial conditions of carriage: regular pickup and delivery hours 6:00 AM to 6:00 PM; waiting-time free time on pickups and deliveries by billed weight (1-500 lb 15 min, 501-9,999 lb 30 min, 10,000-19,999 lb 1 h) then $25.25 per 15 min; attempted pickup charge $4.25/cwt, minimum $45; carrier provides only one employee (the driver) per vehicle and the consignor loads large or heavy articles; tailgate service up to 1,500 lb per lift; carrier liability $2.00/lb ($4.41/kg) unless higher value declared on the bill of lading; all shipments subject to re-weigh and measurement audit with a $25 rescale fee per pro; bill of lading changes must be authorised in writing; dangerous goods surcharge and excluded classes.

assumptions: Channel shares (35% phone or email to the terminal, 10% central customer service, 37% portal or EDI, 18% standing daily pickups) are the author's estimates for 2019-2022; no source gave channel shares for Canadian LTL carriers.
Same-day cutoffs come from two current carrier pages and are assumed to match 2019-2022 practice.
The case ends when the pickup is on the board for its date; a pickup moved to the next business day counts as booked, and the wait until the next day is not part of this process.
Credit-hold release time depends on collections; it is modelled as a wait on the customer service step rather than a separate collections step.

Staffing check: roles state 45.5 FTE, while simulated hands-on time times 100,000 requests implies about 62 FTE at 130 productive hours a month. The gap is within the check's range; clerks on extended-hours shifts work more than 130 hours on the floor, and some terminal clerks shown under other processes (tracing, driver check-in) also take pickup calls at peak.
